\[
Q_t = \{\text{connected } x : I(x) \le t\},
\qquad
v(Q_t) = \frac{\lvert Q_{t + \Delta} \rvert - \lvert Q_{t - \Delta} \rvert}{\lvert Q_t \rvert},
\qquad
\Delta = 5
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(Q_t\): An extremal region at threshold t
- \(v\): The variation, the relative change of the area
- \(\Delta\): Delta, the range of gray levels

Picture the threshold t sweeping the gray levels from black to white. The pixels at or below t form connected regions, which appear, grow and merge. Each one is an extremal region, since all its pixels are darker than every pixel on its border. Matas et al. measure how fast its area changes with v. A region where v has a local minimum is maximally stable: it keeps its shape while the threshold moves. Sweeping the other way gives the bright regions, and OpenCV finds both in one run. Regions outside the area limits, or with v above the most variation, are dropped. Of nested regions that are nearly the same, only one stays. The table gives each region's centroid, the radius of a disk of the same area, and its long axis from the second moments of its pixels.
